I was born in Budapest in 1903. My family used to say that at six I could divide eight-digit numbers in my head and astonish our guests. Later, mathematics became my language. From 1933 I worked at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton — in the same building as Albert Einstein.
h.Ikkinchi jahon urushi boshlanganda men h: When the Second World War began, I became a consultant to military projects, including the atomic project at Los Alamos. There I understood one truth very clearly: our greatest enemy was calculation. To learn how a blast wave spreads took millions of arithmetic operations. In passing he mentioned that in Philadelphia an electronic machine was being built that could do more than 300 multiplications per second. Three hundred per second! I buried him in questions — he later laughed that the conversation turned into something like a doctoral exam. That day a new chapter of my life began. And of the computing machine, too.

I knew his work and valued it highly. My scheme was the engineering form of that idea.

h.<strong>Jorj Bul<\/strong> — Angliyadagi: George Boole was the son of an ordinary English shoemaker and taught himself mathematics. In 1854 he published The Laws of Thought. In it he turned logic into algebra: marking "true" as 1 and "false" as 0, he showed that thoughts could be calculated like numbers. This is called Boolean algebra. For almost 80 years it was seen as pure philosophy — nobody saw a practical use for it.
h.1937-yilda MIT'ning 21 yoshli talabasi <: In 1937, a 21-year-old MIT student, Claude Shannon, showed something astonishing in his master's thesis: circuits of electric switches (relays) obey Boolean algebra exactly. Two switches connected in series give "AND"; connected in parallel they give "OR". Switch closed — current flows — 1. Switch open — no current — 0. With that, logic became electricity. It may well be one of the most useful master's theses in history.

A transistor is a tiny switch controlled by current: apply a voltage to its input and it opens. A modern processor has tens of billions of them. A few transistors make a logic gate — the smallest "thinking" device, which takes one or two bits and returns one bit.

h.Sxemamning kuchi — soddaligida. Uning za: My design's strength is its simplicity. Its weak point is right there too. Both instructions and data travel from memory to the processor along one road — the bus. However fast the processor is, it has to wait its turn on this narrow road for every instruction and every number. Year after year processors got faster much more quickly than memory, and the gap kept growing.
h.Bu muammoga nom bergan — FORTRAN tilinin: The problem was named by John Backus, the creator of FORTRAN. Accepting the Turing Award in 1977, he called it the "von Neumann bottleneck". The solution had been proposed in 1965 by EDSAC's creator, Maurice Wilkes: put a small but very fast "helper memory" next to the processor. Today it's called a cache. The first commercial computer with a cache was the IBM System/360 Model 85 in 1968.

h.<b>Teg tarixi · Tim hikoya qiladi<\/b>Bu: Tag story · Tim tells itI didn't invent most of these tags from scratch. At CERN, scientists wrote documents in a language called SGMLguid, a member of the SGML family. I took the angle brackets and the open-and-close tags from there — people accept familiar things faster. <title> was on my very first list of tags in 1991: I believed every document should have a name. <!DOCTYPE> is also an inheritance from SGML.
h.<b>Teg tarixi · Tim hikoya qiladi<\/b>Sa: Tag story · Tim tells itI didn't invent headings either — they came ready-made from SGMLguid. Physicists' papers had chapters, sections and subsections, so six levels were needed. I didn't change the number. More than thirty years have passed, yet h1–h6 have stayed almost exactly the same. Things that are well thought out live long.
h.<b>Teg tarixi · Tim hikoya qiladi<\/b><c: Tag story · Tim tells it<p> has a curious history. In the first HTML it didn't wrap the text — it was a separator mark placed between two paragraphs, and it had no closing tag. Later, as HTML developed, <p> became a box that wraps text from beginning to end. <br> and <hr> weren't on my first list — they were added a little later, when people tried to write poems and addresses.
h.<b>Teg tarixi · Tim hikoya qiladi<\/b>Me: Tag story · Tim tells itI always had one principle: let HTML say what the text means, and let the browser decide how it looks. <b> only says "make it bold". <strong> says "this is important". Screen readers that read pages aloud for blind people can't see the screen, but they "understand" <strong> and read the word with emphasis. The web is for everyone — so choose the tag that carries meaning.
h.<b>Teg tarixi · Tim hikoya qiladi<\/b>Ol: Tag story · Tim tells itScientists love lists: experiment steps, equipment, conclusions. So the bulleted list (ul and li) was among my first tags in 1991 — it came from SGMLguid too. The numbered list <ol> was added a little later: people got tired of typing "1, 2, 3" by hand and wanted the browser to count for them.
h.<b>Teg tarixi · Tim hikoya qiladi<\/b>Ma: Tag story · Tim tells itHere it is, my favorite tag! I often borrowed the other tags ready-made, but <a> is the heart of the web — I built the whole system for exactly this. The letter a stands for anchor: a link ties you to another document like an anchor. And href means hypertext reference. The word "hypertext" was coined by Ted Nelson in the 1960s. I made one important decision: links would be one-way. You can link to any page without asking its owner for permission. Other systems had tried two-way links, but they became far too complicated. It was exactly this simplicity that let the web grow so fast.
h.<b>Teg tarixi · Tim hikoya qiladi<\/b>Bu: Tag story · Tim tells itI didn't create this tag — and it's one of the most famous stories of the web. February 25, 1993. Marc Andreessen, a young student working at NCSA in the USA, wrote to the web developers' mailing list proposing a new IMG tag for showing images inside text. Others started debating: someone suggested another name, someone advised thinking of a more general solution. But Marc didn't wait — he added the tag to his Mosaic browser and shipped it. Pages suddenly became colorful and alive, and ordinary people fell in love with the web. That's how <img> made it into the standard. The alt attribute was added later — so that everyone, including blind people, could use the web.
h.<b>Startup ustozi<\/b>Mark Andrissenni e: Startup mentorRemember Marc Andreessen: he didn't wait "until everyone agreed" — he put something working into people's hands. A year later he started Netscape. Startups work the same way: a working first version matters more than a perfect plan.
h.<b>Teg tarixi · Tim hikoya qiladi<\/b>Bu: Tag story · Tim tells itThis notation is also inherited from SGML. Now a funny story: not all tags lived long. In 1994 the Netscape browser added the <blink> tag — it made text flash on and off. According to Netscape engineer Lou Montulli, the idea was born as a joke among friends, and then someone actually programmed it. The result? The whole web filled up with blinking text and everyone got sick of it. The tag never made it into an official standard, and in 2013 even Firefox stopped supporting it. The lesson: adding a tag is easy; adding a useful tag is hard.
h.<b>Ustoz maslahati<\/b>Agar signal chiqm: Mentor's tipIf no signal shows up, that's not a failure — it's months saved. Better to spend three days talking and find out there's no problem than to code for a month and find out then. Take the next one from your problem notebook.
h.<b>Fon Neyman o'ylaydi<\/b>Tasavvur qili: Von Neumann reflectsImagine the fastest cook in the world — but for every new dish, the kitchen has to be rebuilt for him. Cooking takes a minute; rebuilding the kitchen takes a week. The problem isn't the cook — the problem is there's nowhere to keep the recipe.
h.<b>Qiziq fakt<\/b>Faqat bitta turdagi da: Fun factFrom just one type of gate — NAND (AND + NOT) — you can build all the others. So in theory, an entire computer can be built from a single kind of brick.
h.<b>3-dars bilan bog'liqlik<\/b>ASCII'da: Connection to Lesson 3ASCII had no Uzbek o' or g', and no Russian or Chinese letters. In 1992 Ken Thompson and Rob Pike created UTF-8: it fits every writing system in the world without breaking ASCII. The <meta charset="UTF-8"> you wrote in Lesson 3 tells the browser exactly that.
h.<b>Oshxona misoli<\/b>Protsessor — oshpa: The kitchen analogyThe processor is the cook. A register is the knife in his hand. The cache is the counter next to the stove. RAM is the fridge in another room. The disk is a warehouse on the edge of town. However quick the cook is, if he runs to the fridge for every onion, dinner will be late. A cache means bringing the things you need often to the counter in advance.
h.<b>Startup ustozi<\/b>E'tibor bering: ve: Startup mentorNotice: the web didn't start from an idea but from a real problem seen every day. And the customers were the colleagues next door. That's exactly the "problem → solution → customer" rule from Lesson 1.
h.<b>Startup ustozi<\/b>Netscape 1994-yild: Startup mentorNetscape was founded in 1994 and went public in 1995, stunning the whole world. A young programmer built one of the most famous startups in history with a single browser.
